Its former shrine rank was {{ill|Gō-sha|Q134917316|qid=Q134917316}}. {{nihongo|'''Ōmatonotsunoten Shrine'''|大麻止乃豆乃天神社}} is a [[shinto shrine]] in the [[Engishiki Jinmyōchō]]. It is located in [[Musashi Province]].

== Enshrined deities ==
; Main sanctuary
* {{ill|Kushimachi no Mikoto|ja|櫛真智命|qid=Q108039939}} (くしまちのみこと)
: A deity said to be the father of Ame-no-Sokotachi no Mikoto<ref name="watarai">Junzaburō Hayakawa, “Watarai-shi Keizu,” *Keizu Sōran*, vol. 2, Kokushokankōkai, 1915, p. 396.</ref>. In the *Engishiki Jinmyōchō*, the entry for the Ame-no-Kagu-yama-ni-masu Kushimachi no Mikoto Shrine in {{ill|Toichi district|ja|十市郡|zh|十市郡|qid=Q11405036}}, {{ill|Yamato Province|Q907495|qid=Q907495}} (present-day {{ill|Amanokaguyama Shrine|Q98082987|qid=Q98082987}}, located on the northern foothills of {{ill|Mount Amanokagu|Q11443780|qid=Q11443780}} in {{ill|Kashihara, Nara|Q496319|qid=Q496319}}, Nara Prefecture) includes the note “former name: Ōmatonochi no Kami.” From this, it has been considered that this shrine enshrines the same deity as Amekaguyama Shrine. Until the {{ill|Edo period|ar|فترة إيدو|ast|Periodu Edo|az|Edo dövrü|bcl|Panahon nin Edo|be|Перыяд Эда|bg|Едо (период)|bn|এদো যুগ|bo|ཨེ་དོའི་དུས་སྐབས།|br|Marevezh Edo|ca|Període Edo|ckb|سەردەمی ئێدۆ|cs|Období Edo|cv|Эдо тапхăрĕ|da|Edo-perioden|de|Edo-Zeit|eo|Epoko de Edo|es|Período Edo|et|Edo ajastu|eu|Edo aroa|fa|دوره ادو|fi|Edo-kausi|fr|Époque d'Edo|gl|Período Edo|he|תקופת אדו|hi|एदो अवधी|hr|Edo (razdoblje)|hu|Edo-kor|id|Zaman Edo|is|Jedótímabilið|it|Periodo Edo|ja|江戸時代|jv|Jaman Édo|ko|에도 시대|lt|Edo laikotarpis|lv|Edo periods|mk|Едо (период)|mn|Эдогийн эрин|ms|Zaman Edo|nl|Edoperiode|nn|Edotida|oc|Periòde Edo|pl|Edo (okres)|pt|Período Edo|ro|Perioada Edo|ru|Период Эдо|simple|Edo period|sk|Obdobie Edo|sl|Obdobje Edo|sq|Periudha Edo|sr|Едо период|su|Période Edo|sv|Edoperioden|th|ยุคเอโดะ|tl|Panahong Edo|tok|tenpo pi kulupu lawa Eto|tr|Edo Dönemi|uk|Період Едо|ur|ایڈو دور|uz|Edo davri|vi|Thời kỳ Edo|war|Panahon Edo|wuu|江戶時代|zh|江户时代|zh_min_nan|Edo sî-tāi|zh_yue|江戶時代|qid=Q184963}}, the shrine was called Marumiya Myōjin, which is said to be a corruption of “Matono-no-miya Myōjin”{{sfn|Shinpen Musashi Fudoki-kō Ōmaru Village}}.

== History ==
[[Image:Torii of Oomatono Tsunoten Shinto Shrine in Inagi taken in May 2009.jpg|thumb|180px|Torii gate (May 2009)]]
[[Image:Komainu in Oomatono Tsunoten Shinto Shrine in Inagi taken in May 2009.jpg|thumb|180px|Komainu. Inscribed “An auspicious day in the sixth month of the twelfth year of {{ill|Tenpō|Q1369045|qid=Q1369045}}, {{ill|Yin Metal Ox|Q904956|qid=Q904956}}” ({{ill|1841|Q7622|qid=Q7622}}). (May 2009)]]
[[Image:View from Oomatono Tsunoten Shinto Shrine in Inagi taken in May 2009.jpg|thumb|180px|View from the precincts over the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=alluvial plain}} of the middle reaches of the {{ill|Tama River|Q1063006|qid=Q1063006}}. {{ill|Inagi Bridge|Q11596545|qid=Q11596545}} can be seen spanning the Tama River. (May 2009)]]
Although it is a very small shrine and its origins are unclear, the *{{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Report on Shikinaisha Investigations}}* identifies this shrine as the “Ōmatono Tsunoten Tenjin Shrine” listed in the *{{ill|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|Q11064932|qid=Q11064932}}* for {{ill|Tama district|Q11430789|qid=Q11430789}}, {{ill|Musashi Province|Q907398|qid=Q907398}}. However, regarding the Shikinaisha Ōmatono Tsunoten Tenjin Shrine, {{ill|Musashi-Mitake Shrine|Q6587276|qid=Q6587276}} in {{ill|Ōme, Tokyo|Q237683|qid=Q237683}}, Tokyo, is also considered a {{ill|Shikinai Ronsha|Q135022904|qid=Q135022904}}, and in the early {{ill|Meiji era|Q3125096|qid=Q3125096}} Musashi Mitake Shrine was known as Ōmatono Tsunoten Tenjin Shrine.

The name “Ōmatono-tsu” is thought to mean “a landing place on a large, round, flat plain”<ref>Inagi City Board of Education (ed.), *Inagi no Chimei to Kyūdō*, p. 73.</ref>. In fact, the former place name of the lowland in front of {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Fumon Zen’an}} adjacent to the shrine precincts was “Irigata,” and it was a {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=lagoon}} of the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Old Tama River}} sandwiched between Tenjin-yama and Shiro-yama (which contains remains of a {{ill|Muromachi period|Q334845|qid=Q334845}} fort).

The place name Ōmaru in Inagi City, where this shrine stands, is also said to mean “large, round, flat plain.” This area has been one of the river-crossing points of the {{ill|Tama River|Q1063006|qid=Q1063006}} since ancient times (where the {{ill|Fuchū Highway|Q11486060|qid=Q11486060}} and the Kawasaki Highway converge), so it is reasonable to think that there was a {{ill|river port|Q11555884|qid=Q11555884}} here. Incidentally, the aforementioned Shiro-yama is also thought to have been built to control the Tama River crossing.

== On-site information ==
;Address
* 847 {{ill|Ōmaru|ja|大丸 (稲城市)|qid=Q30923766|lt=Ōmaru}}, {{ill|Inagi|ar|إناغي (طوكيو)|azb|ایناقی، توکیو|ca|Inagi|ce|Инаги|ceb|Inagi-shi|cs|Inagi|de|Inagi|el|Ινάγκι (Τόκιο)|eo|Inagi|es|Inagi (Tokio)|et|Inagi|eu|Inagi|fa|ایناگی، توکیو|fi|Inagi|fr|Inagi|gl|Inagi|hy|Ինագի|id|Inagi, Tōkyō|it|Inagi|ja|稲城市|ko|이나기시|lt|Inagis|ms|Inagi|mzn|ایناگی، توکیو|nl|Inagi|pl|Inagi|pt|Inagi|ro|Inagi|ru|Инаги|su|Inagi, Tokyo|sv|Inagi|tg|Инаги|th|อินางิ|tl|Inagi|tr|Inagi|tt|Инаги|tum|Inagi|uk|Інаґі|ur|ایناگی|vi|Inagi, Tokyo|war|Inagi|zh|稻城市|zh_classical|稻城市|zh_min_nan|Inagi-chhī|zh_yue|稻城市|qid=Q317847}}, {{ill|Tokyo|Q1490|qid=Q1490}}

;Access
* Nearest station: About an 8-minute walk (approx. 600 m south) from {{ill|Minami-Tama Station|Q5366901|qid=Q5366901}} on the JR {{ill|Nambu Line|Q1366263|qid=Q1366263}}

;Surroundings
Located on the northern edge of the central {{ill|Tama Hills|Q1502721|qid=Q1502721}}, the shrine offers a panoramic view from its precincts of the {{ill|alluvial plain of the middle reaches of the Tama River|Q131910796|qid=Q131910796|lt=alluvial plain of the middle reaches of the Tama River}}. The wooded hill behind the precincts was formerly called Shiro-yama; in the medieval period, a mountain castle known as Ōmaru Castle, a {{ill|Hill castle|Q15710038|qid=Q15710038}}, was built there. Today, the area forms part of the {{ill|Tama New Town|Q7680510|qid=Q7680510}} {{ill|Kōyōdai|Q11416047|qid=Q11416047|lt=Kōyōdai}} residential district. Along both sides of the approach to the shrine are the Buddhist temples Enshō-ji and Jikishin-an, and to the north of the precincts is another Buddhist temple, Fumon Zen’an.
